summary: Defines an extension to the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) that represents the capabilities of a SIP user agent. This lets presence information tell others what the user's device can do. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Presence says if a friend is online. This adds a note about what their device can do, like voice, video or chat.

questions: sip user agent capabilities in pidf
what is the pidf user agent capability extension
how does presence show sip device capabilities
subtitle: A set of XML elements that lets a presence document say what a SIP device or service can actually do.

tldr.problem: A presence document normally gives only a contact address, and a SIP URI can stand for voice, video or messaging, so watchers cannot tell what kind of communication will work.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps the SIP user agent capability feature tags into XML elements: the servcaps element describes a service and the devcaps element describes a device, both placed inside a PIDF presence document.
tldr.outcome: Watchers get hints about a presentity's capabilities before they try to communicate, but the hints do not replace SIP capability negotiation.

today: RFC 5196 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of this PIDF capability extension.

sections.title: Why Presence Needs Capabilities
sections.content:
The Presence Information Data Format (PIDF, RFC 3863) is deliberately minimal. Its <contact> element holds a single URI. For some schemes that is enough to know the service, since an im: URI usually means instant messaging. A SIP URI is different: it can reach voice, video or messaging services, so a watcher seeing only a SIP URI may not know what the tuple describes.

This RFC fills the gap with a SIP-specific extension that carries the same media feature tags as RFC 3840. SIP-based presence applications can then publish richer information than baseline PIDF.

The scope is limited. The extension does not replace media negotiation such as SDP. Its purpose is to give watchers hints about the presentity's preferences, willingness and capabilities before they start to communicate.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone number alone does not tell you if someone can take a video call. This adds a label that says what the line can do.

sections.title: Service and Device Capabilities
sections.content:
The presence data model in RFC 4479 describes presence as three kinds of data: person, service and device. This RFC follows that model with two XML extensions, one for service capabilities and one for device capabilities. Both use the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:caps.

Besides the features from RFC 3840, the extension adds the type feature tag from RFC 2913, the message media type tag from RFC 4569 and the language tag from RFC 4646. A combined document MUST follow the formatting rules in Section 4.1 of RFC 3863.

The extension is meant for PIDF, but the text says it may also be used with other XML documents if appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of notes: one about the service (like a chat line) and one about the device (like a phone you carry around).

sections.title: Service Capability Elements
sections.content:
Service capabilities sit inside a <servcaps> element, which SHOULD be a child of the PIDF <tuple>. The root element must always be present.

Several children are plain booleans: <audio>, <application>, <data>, <control>, <video>, <text> and <message> say whether a streaming media type is supported. <automata> says whether the service is an automaton such as a voicemail server (true) or a human (false), and <isfocus> says whether it is a conference server. <type> holds a MIME type of the form type/subtype, and <description> is text that SHOULD carry an xml:lang attribute, defaulting to i-default.

Other children are lists with <supported> and <notsupported> sub-elements:

  • <class>: business, personal.
  • <duplex>: full, half, receive-only, send-only.
  • <actor>: principal, attendant, msg-taker, information.
  • <event-packages>, <methods> and <extensions>: values from the matching IANA SIP registries, such as INVITE or MESSAGE for methods.
  • <schemes> (with <s> children) and <languages> (with <l> children).
  • <priority>: <lowerthan maxvalue>, <higherthan minvalue>, <equals value> and <range minvalue maxvalue>.

Most of these elements can also be followed by extension elements from other namespaces, which is how the format can grow.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a checklist. Some boxes are yes or no, like video. Others are lists of what works and what does not.

sections.title: Device Capability Elements
sections.content:
Device capabilities go in a <devcaps> element, which SHOULD be a child of the <device> element from the presence data model. It can contain <mobility> and <description>, followed by extension elements from other namespaces.

<mobility> uses the <supported> and <notsupported> pattern with two values: <fixed> (stationary) and <mobile> (can move with the user). A device is fixed if it has a fixed point of contact with the network, so the text notes that cordless phones count as fixed. The <description> element works as it does for services.
sections.plainLanguage: For the device, the note says whether it stays put, like a desk phone, or goes with you, like a mobile.

sections.title: Usage Guidelines
sections.content:
The published capabilities need not match reality. A presentity may not want to reveal that it supports voice, and server authorization policies or the merging of information from several sources can alter or lose details. Even so, the RFC says it is in the presentity's interest to publish accurate information, to reduce failed attempts to communicate. Watchers should not expect the information to be fully aligned with the true capabilities, and SIP signalling is still the way to negotiate.

Presence User Agents (PUAs) are RECOMMENDED to provide information as complete as they can. If the data is sensitive, a PUA SHOULD get permission from the presentity.

PUAs should list items under <supported> and <notsupported> only when it helps the watcher decide. A message service that supports MESSAGE should list it as supported, but listing every unsupported method adds little. If the same value appears in both lists, the watcher can safely assume it is supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is a hint, not a promise. Say what really helps, and if the note contradicts itself, believe the yes.

sections.title: An Example Document
sections.content:
The RFC includes one full presence document for pres:someone@example.com. Its tuple has an open basic status and a <servcaps> block with audio true, video false, message true, full duplex, the methods ACK, BYE, INVITE and MESSAGE, priority lower than 10, the scheme sip, and descriptions in English and Hungarian. The contact is sip:someone@example.com.

A separate <device> element carries a <devcaps> block saying the device is mobile.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is a filled-in card: voice and chat yes, video no, and the phone is a mobile one.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content: All security considerations of RFC 3859 and RFC 3863 apply. Compared with plain PIDF, this format may reveal more about a user's services and devices. For that reason a PUA SHOULD always obtain permission from the presentity when publishing sensitive information with this extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The note tells people more about you, so ask first before sharing it.
